credits.name: Arkansas personal tax credits (§ 26-51-501, AR1000F line 31)

notes: ARKANSAS'S HIGHEST MARGINAL RATE IS 13.70%, AND IT IS NOT IN ARKANSAS'S RATE SCHEDULE. A.C.A. § 26-51-201 has TWO schedules selected by income: a filer whose net taxable income does not exceed $94,700 pays the graduated table, and a filer one dollar above it pays 2% on the first $4,700 plus the top rate on every dollar above that, applied to their WHOLE net income, less a bracket adjustment of $290 that falls by $10 for each further $100 of income. A $10 relief withdrawn per $100 earned is ten percentage points of marginal rate, so the band from $94,701 to $97,600 is taxed at 13.70% in 2026 and the 2025 band from $94,701 to $97,800 at 13.90% — against top statutory rates of 3.7% and 3.9%. Nothing in any published Arkansas bracket table contains either figure.

AND THE BRACKET ADJUSTMENT IS A STAIRCASE OF THIRTY CLIFFS RATHER THAN A SLOPE. Its rows are $100 wide and its amounts are whole dollars, so the tax steps rather than rises: $10 of Arkansas tax arrives on one cent of income, 29 times in 2026 and 31 times in 2025. A provision written to stop a cliff at $94,700 is itself thirty smaller cliffs. In 2026 it also OVERSHOOTS: the tax at $94,700 is $3,136.70 and at $94,701 it is $3,134.04, so one dollar of extra income CUTS the bill by $2.66, where the 2025 card undershoots the same join by $20.70. The provision changed sign between the two years and no act changed it — the 2026 amount is Act 1 of 2026's and the 2025 one is the Department of Finance and Administration's.

A MODEL BUILT FROM ARKANSAS'S PUBLISHED BRACKET TABLE ALONE IS TOO LOW BY A FLAT $287.30 FOR EVERY FILER ABOVE THE ADJUSTMENT BAND. Every account of this state prints the graduated schedule — 0%, 2%, 3%, 3.4%, 3.7% at $5,600, $11,200, $16,000 and $26,400 — and stops there. Above $97,600 the high-income table has taken over and the bracket adjustment has reached zero, so the two routes differ by the whole adjustment and the error does not depend on income: it is $287.30 at $100,000 and $287.30 at $10,000,000. The 2025 card needs TWO figures rather than one — $330.70 from $97,801 to $100,000 and $329.00 above $100,001 — because for $100,001 and over DFA prints "$3,809 plus 3.9% of the excess over $100,000", a reduction of $91.00 where the row beneath carries $89.30, so an Arkansan earning one dollar more than $100,000 pays $1.70 LESS. `tools/cross-package/arkansas-bracket-adjustment.mjs` asserts all three figures, the 13.70% slope and the direction on every push.

THE LOW INCOME TAX TABLES CHARGE THE POOREST ARKANSANS UP TO 12.40%, WHICH IS 3.37 TIMES THE STATE'S TOP RATE. § 26-51-301 and the AR1000F instructions give seven tables of tax by state AGI and family size, taken IN LIEU of the standard or itemized deduction whenever they come out lower. Below an exempt amount the tax is nothing — $14,643 for a single filer, $29,722 for a couple with two or more dependents — and above it the table's own implied marginal rate is 7.00% single, 9.40% head of household with no or one dependent, 10.40% joint with no or one, 10.77% joint with two or more and 12.40% HEAD OF HOUSEHOLD WITH TWO OR MORE. The steepest rate in the Arkansas income tax is charged to a single parent of two earning between $24,818 and $29,000. All five figures are measured from the tables in `test/arkansas.test.js` rather than stated.

AND THE TABLES ARE READ ON STATE AGI, NOT ON TAXABLE INCOME, BECAUSE THEY REPLACE THE DEDUCTION. A model that looks the table up on income after the standard deduction understates every household that uses it: $2,470 of deduction is 24 of a single filer's 29 taxed rows. This package computes both routes and takes the lower, which is what the reference model does; the instructions phrase it as an eligibility test instead, and the two agree because the table is below the schedule wherever it reaches. MARRIED FILING SEPARATELY IS BARRED FROM ALL SEVEN TABLES, so a separated Arkansan at $14,000 of AGI pays tax on $14,000 less $2,470 where a single filer at the same income pays nothing at all.

THE LOW INCOME TAX TABLES ARE STAIRCASES TOO, AND SO IS THE ADDITIONAL TAX CREDIT, WHICH MAKES FOUR ON ONE RETURN. The low income tax table rows are $100 wide with whole-dollar amounts, so $4 to $13 of tax arrives on one dollar of income between 28 and 63 times per table. The Additional Tax Credit for Qualified Individuals is $60 ($120 joint) at or below $26,500 of net taxable income, withdrawn by $5 for each $100 "OR PART OF" $100 above it — the ceiling, not the quotient, so it is twelve steps of $5 rather than a 5% phase-out, and gone at $27,700. Counting the 2025 rate card's own thirty-one-row reduction taper, an Arkansas return has something over three hundred incomes at which one more dollar costs between $4 and $13.

ARKANSAS'S PUBLISHED RATE CARD AND ARKANSAS'S STATUTE DO NOT COMPUTE THE SAME TAX, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE ROW'S RATE ON ONE DOLLAR. For 2025 the tax is the row's rate on all net taxable income minus the row's "minus adjustment", and those adjustments are $111.98, $223.97, $287.97 and $419.96 where the accumulated tax of the bands beneath is $112.00, $224.00, $288.00 and $420.00. Each shortfall is exactly the row's rate applied to one dollar: 0.02 x 5,599 = 111.98 and 0.039 x 26,399 - 609.60 = 419.96. The card is anchored one dollar below each bracket floor, so EVERY Arkansan above $5,600 pays the graduated statutory tax plus two to four cents. The instructions settle which governs — a formula's results "must match the table" — so the cents are real, and the reference model agrees: policyengine-us carried the round figures as late as 2.15.3 and replaced them with the card's by 2.68.0.

THE RETIREMENT EXEMPTION HAS NO AGE TEST AND HAS NOT MOVED SINCE 1997. § 26-51-307 exempts $6,000 per recipient of employment-related pension and IRA distribution income at ANY age, and nothing indexes it; a 45-year-old Arkansan with a $20,000 pension exempts $6,000 of it. It is claimed PER PERSON on the recipient's own income, so pass `retirement.filer` and `retirement.spouse` separately — a couple whose $12,000 of pension is all in one name exempts $6,000 and the same couple with $6,000 each exempts the lot. Military retired pay is exempt IN FULL from tax year 2018 under Act 141 of 2017 and does NOT consume the $6,000, which is Oklahoma's treatment and not South Carolina's.

NOT MODELLED — THE "65 SPECIAL" SECOND AGED CREDIT, AND IT IS AN ELECTION RATHER THAN AN OMISSION. § 26-51-501 gives a filer of 65 or over a second $29 personal credit ONLY IF they did not use the $6,000 retirement exemption, which the AR1000F prints as a box of its own. So an elderly Arkansan with a pension chooses between $6,000 of exemption and $29 of credit, and the choice turns at $783.78 of pension income: below it the credit is worth more. This package allows the credit only where no retirement exemption is claimed, which is what the reference model does and which does NOT optimise the election — so an Arkansas figure from here is TOO HIGH by up to $28.96, for a filer of 65 with a trivial pension, and by nothing for anybody else. Supplying the pension through `subtractions` rather than `retirement` elects the credit.

FIFTY PER CENT OF NET LONG-TERM CAPITAL GAIN IS EXEMPT, WHICH IS THE LARGEST FLAT CAPITAL-GAINS EXCLUSION IN THIS PACKAGE — North Dakota excludes 40%, South Carolina 44%, Wisconsin 30%. § 26-51-815(a) and the AR1000D worksheet exempt half the excess of net long-term capital gain over net short-term capital LOSS, and add short-term GAIN back in full, so the exclusion reaches the long-term half only: pass `netCapitalGain` and `shortTermCapitalGains` separately or a short-term gain is exempted that Arkansas taxes. $100,000 of long-term gain is $50,000 of exemption and $1,850.00 of 2026 tax. WHAT IS NOT MODELLED ALONGSIDE IT: gain above $10,000,000 on a SINGLE TRANSACTION is exempt in full under the same subsection, which needs a per-transaction figure rather than an annual total, and the statutory cap on a deductible net capital LOSS.

ALSO NOT MODELLED, and each would REDUCE an Arkansas return computed here: the child and dependent care credit of 20% of the federal credit; the $29 credit for a DEAF filer, which no field here carries; the $500 credit for a dependent with a developmental disability, likewise; the post-secondary tuition deduction; and the credit for taxes paid to another state. Supply deductions through `subtractions`.

ARKANSAS ITEMIZED DEDUCTIONS ARE NOT MODELLED AND THE ELECTION IS NOT LOCKED TO THE FEDERAL ONE. Arkansas allows itemizing independently of the federal return — unlike Oklahoma, which forces the two to match — and its own Schedule AR3 disallows state income taxes and limits several categories differently from Schedule A. `stateItemizedDeductions` is not read for Arkansas, so a filer who would itemize is computed here on the $2,470 or $4,940 standard deduction instead, and their Arkansas figure from here is TOO HIGH by the excess at their marginal rate.

THE STANDARD DEDUCTION IS $2,470 FOR EVERY STATUS BUT JOINT, WHICH GETS $4,940 — AND A SINGLE PARENT GETS NO MORE THAN A SINGLE FILER. § 26-51-430 set $2,200 and $4,400 in 2015 and indexes them to CPI-U with the result ROUNDED DOWN to the nearest $10, which is why the figures are $2,470 and $4,940 and not a round number. Head of household, married filing separately and a qualifying surviving spouse all take the single amount. It is the second smallest standard deduction among the states in this package that HAVE one — Mississippi's $2,300 is smaller and thirteen states allow none at all — and roughly a sixth of the federal one, which is the arithmetic that makes Arkansas's own low-income tables matter: they are worth more than the deduction to every household they reach.

ARKANSAS TAXES INTEREST ON OTHER STATES' MUNICIPAL BONDS AND EXEMPTS ITS OWN, so an Arkansan holding out-of-state bonds owes Arkansas tax on income THE FEDERAL RETURN NEVER SAW. Pass `outOfStateMunicipalInterest` rather than `taxExemptInterest`: the Arkansas/elsewhere split exists on no federal form and cannot be derived from anything else here, and taking the whole of tax-exempt interest would tax an Arkansan on Arkansas bonds. Omitted, an Arkansas bondholder is too LOW by 3.7% of the out-of-state part — $370.00 on $10,000 — which is the direction this package errs in almost nowhere else. The AR1000ADJ line number for an individual return could not be read from this sandbox; what is established is the rule, from Arkansas's own taxpayer guidance and from the corporate schedule AR1100ADJ, which carries the addition as a line of its own.

NO CITY, COUNTY OR SCHOOL DISTRICT IN ARKANSAS LEVIES AN INCOME TAX. The state figure is the whole of an Arkansas resident's income tax, so `locality` is never required and `SUPPORTED_LOCALITIES` names none here.

ARKANSAS TAXES TIPS AND OVERTIME THAT THE FEDERAL GOVERNMENT NOW EXEMPTS. AR1000F starts from federal gross income rather than federal AGI and Arkansas has legislated no subtraction for the four OBBBA Schedule 1-A deductions — § 224 tips, § 225 overtime, § 151(d)(5) senior and § 163(h)(4) vehicle loan interest — so none of them reaches an Arkansas return. A tipped Arkansas worker with $8,000 of qualified tips pays Arkansas $296.00 in 2026 on income the federal return exempted entirely.

ARKANSAS'S RATE COULD FALL AGAIN AND NOTHING HERE PROJECTS IT. The top individual rate has been cut in each of 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2026 — 5.9% to 4.9% to 4.7% to 3.9% to 3.7% — by four separate acts, two of them in extraordinary sessions called for the purpose. This package ships the schedule Act 1 of 2026 prints. A 2027 Arkansas figure is an act that has not passed, not an indexation that can be computed.

5 figures were supplied and spent on nothing: `federalDeductions`, `filerAge`, `socialSecurityAndMedicarePaid`, `earnedIncome`, `retirement`. Every figure in this result — and every other note in it — is identical to the one this return would have had without them. That is MEASURED rather than looked up: the 2025 Arkansas return was computed again without each field and the answers compared. It does NOT mean Arkansas has no rule that reads the field, because a rule can need two fields together and the other one may be the one that is missing — Ohio reads `earnedIncome` only once `city` is supplied as well. It means nothing on THIS return moved, so a caller who went and looked the figures up bought no change in the answer by it.

credits.name: Kentucky personal tax credit for age 65 or over (Schedule ITC)
Kentucky family size tax credit (Schedule ITC Section C)

notes: Kentucky's rate falls from 4.0% in 2025 to 3.5% in 2026 under HB 1 (2025), a 12.5% cut in the bill. Further reductions are conditional on revenue triggers in KRS 141.020(4) and are not scheduled.

This package applies one standard deduction per return. Kentucky couples commonly file "married filing separately on a combined return" (Form 740 filing status 2), which claims two standard deductions on one form; that is worth $3,270 of deduction, about $131 of tax in 2025, and this package does not model it.

Kentucky does not tax Social Security or Tier 1 railroad retirement benefits. Pass the taxable part — Form 1040 line 6b — as `taxableSocialSecurity` and it comes off the base; do NOT also put it in `subtractions`, or it will be subtracted twice.

The pension income exclusion of KRS 141.019(1) is PER PERSON and is claimed on Schedule P. It covers pensions, annuities, IRA and 401(k) distributions and other written retirement plans alike — Kentucky asks nothing about the character of the income or the form of the account — and it has NO AGE TEST AT ALL. Pass `retirement` with a `filer` and a `spouse`. Of the three states here that exempt retirement income, Kentucky has the smallest headline figure and is the only one a 55-year-old retiree can use: Georgia's exclusion begins at 62 and Maryland's at 65, so a couple who both retire at 55 with $70,000 of pension exclude $62,220 in Kentucky and nothing in either of the others.

The $31,110 is NOT Kentucky's maximum. Retired pay from the federal government, the Commonwealth or a Kentucky local government is exempt IN FULL to the extent it is attributable to service performed before 1 January 1998, with no ceiling — and that exempt amount is not charged against the $31,110, which stays available against everything else. Pass it as `retirement.filer.governmentPension` with `serviceMonthsBefore1998` and `serviceMonthsAfter1997`. A Kentucky teacher who served 1975-2005 with a $70,000 pension and $40,000 of IRA distributions excludes $84,776.67 on a return whose published exclusion is $31,110.

Military retired pay is federal service, so it belongs in `governmentPension` with the months: a Kentucky military retiree who served before 1998 has the same uncapped exemption as a state employee. Do not put it in `militaryRetirement`, which is Maryland's and Georgia's field and is not read here.

The 1 January 1998 cutoff has never moved, which makes the uncapped exemption a closed cohort emptying by retirement — the same shape as Virginia's untested age deduction for filers born before 1939. It also means every further month of service DILUTES the exempt percentage, because the denominator grows and the numerator cannot: a Kentucky employee hired in 1988 was 100% exempt if they retired in 1997 and is 25% exempt if they retire in 2027. The exempt DOLLARS are roughly unchanged, because a pension earned over more months is larger; it is the taxable remainder that grows.

The $31,110 is the only figure in this package other than Maryland's exclusion that has ever gone DOWN, and it fell much further. It was indexed from $35,700 in 1999 to $41,110 in 2005, frozen there for thirteen years, cut by 24% to $31,110 by the 2018 reform, and frozen again. It is not indexed, so it has lost roughly half its real value since it was last set — and the rate cut from 4.0% to 3.5% cuts what is left of it by a further 12.5%.

The personal tax credit for age (KRS 141.020(3), Schedule ITC) is $40 for the filer and $40 for a spouse on the return, at 65 or over, with NO INCOME TEST — computed here from v0.61.0 and not before. Until then every Kentucky filer 65 or over was overstated by $40, and every elderly couple by $80. It was found by `tools/anchors`, which reproduces a figure read off a filled return rather than off another model: the engine's own unread-input note had been reporting `filerAge` as "supplied and spent on nothing" on every Kentucky return, which is exactly what a missing age credit looks like, and nothing read it.

The $31,110 is the only figure in this package other than Maryland's exclusion that has ever gone DOWN, and it fell much further. It was indexed from $35,700 in 1999 to $41,110 in 2005, frozen there for thirteen years, cut by 24% to $31,110 by the 2018 reform, and frozen again. It is not indexed, so it has lost roughly half its real value since it was last set — and the rate cut from 4.0% to 3.5% cuts what is left of it by a further 12.5%.

The personal tax credit for age (KRS 141.020(3), Schedule ITC) is $40 for the filer and $40 for a spouse on the return, at 65 or over, with NO INCOME TEST — computed here from v0.61.0 and not before. Until then every Kentucky filer 65 or over was overstated by $40, and every elderly couple by $80. It was found by `tools/anchors`, which reproduces a figure read off a filled return rather than off another model: the engine's own unread-input note had been reporting `filerAge` as "supplied and spent on nothing" on every Kentucky return, which is exactly what a missing age credit looks like, and nothing read it.

NOT MODELLED — the other two personal tax credits in the same subsection. KRS 141.020(3)(a)6 allows $40 for a filer or spouse who is LEGALLY BLIND, so a filer who is both 65 and blind claims $80 per person and this package pays $40; the blockage is the input and not the statute, because `blindOrDisabled` counts blind and disabled filers together — which is right for Michigan's special exemption, whose statute covers both — and reading it here would pay a blindness credit to a filer who is disabled and sighted. KRS 141.020(3)(a)8 allows a further $20, and THIS PACKAGE DOES NOT KNOW WHAT IT IS FOR: Schedule ITC Section B is where it is claimed, the reference model keys it on having military service income and labels it a military-service credit, and Kentucky's own form has historically carried a Kentucky National Guard box. No Kentucky document resolves from this sandbox to settle which, so the amount is stated and the condition is not. Supply either through `subtractions` grossed up by the rate.

THE FAMILY SIZE TAX CREDIT (KRS 141.066, Schedule ITC Section C) is computed here from v0.62.0 and not before, and it was the largest gap in any state this package ships because it is a percentage of the WHOLE TAX. At or below a threshold amount set at the federal poverty guideline for the family size — $15,650, $21,150, $26,650 and $32,150 for sizes one to four in 2025 — it forgives 100% of the Kentucky tax, and it steps down to nothing at 133% of that figure. Until v0.62.0 a single Kentucky filer at exactly $15,650 was charged $495.20, which was the entire bill, and one at $8,000 was charged $189.20. The maximum family size is four (KRS 141.066(1)(e)4), so a fifth person moves nothing, and the credit applies to the tax REMAINING AFTER the $40 personal credits rather than to the tax before them — taking the percentage first would produce a negative tax on a credit that is not refundable.

THE CUTOFFS ARE WHOLE DOLLARS AND THE BAND IS "NOT OVER", WHICH IS WHY THIS PACKAGE CARRIES 127 AND 133 WHERE THE LEADING OPEN MODEL CARRIES 1.270032 AND 1.330032. Kentucky prints the grid in dollars, so the comparison is against `round(percent x threshold)`. Every 2025 threshold amount is an odd multiple of $50, and of the ten statutory percentages exactly TWO multiply a multiple of $50 into something other than a whole number: 127% and 133%, which land on $.50 at all four family sizes and round up — $19,875.50 prints as $19,876. Those are precisely the two steps `policyengine-us` perturbs, and 130% sitting unfitted between them is the proof, because 130% of a multiple of $50 is whole. The two readings agree at EVERY integer income in 2025. They disagree at eleven in 2026, where the guideline is $15,960 and $5,680 and eight of the ten percentages produce a fractional cutoff: a household of three at $34,697 and of four at $41,911 and $43,891 get a step less here, and eight others get a step more, each worth ten percentage points of the whole bill. A constant fitted to one year is not a rounding rule, so this package takes the rule that explains the printed grid; `test/kentucky-family-size-credit.test.js` enumerates all eleven.

UNVERIFIED — WHETHER THE CUTOFF IS ROUNDED HALF UP OR ROUNDED UP. All eight of the 2025 cells that settle the direction land on exactly $.50, so round-half-up and ceiling reproduce every one of them and nothing in that year discriminates between the two. This package rounds half up. The question only has an answer in a year whose cutoffs land somewhere other than $.50, which 2026 is at three of the four family sizes, and no Kentucky document resolves from this sandbox to settle it — so 2026 cutoffs at a fractional product other than $.50 are a reading rather than a reproduction.

MODIFIED GROSS INCOME, the figure this credit is banded on, is the LARGER of federal AGI and Kentucky AGI and not either one of them. That is the whole reason it is a base of its own: Kentucky AGI is normally the smaller figure, because the KRS 141.019(1) pension exclusion and the Social Security subtraction come out of it, and taking the larger stops a Kentucky subtraction from buying eligibility for a credit that can forgive the entire bill — a retiree with $30,000 of pension has almost no Kentucky AGI and gets nothing here. Absent `kentuckyModifiedGrossIncome` this package derives `max(federal AGI, Kentucky AGI)`, which is EXACT for a return with no lump-sum distribution and no out-of-state municipal bond interest, and a FLOOR otherwise: worksheet line (c), tax-exempt interest on other states' municipal bonds, and line (d), a Form 4972 lump sum that is in no AGI at all, are both added on the form and neither is added here. A floor on the income is a CEILING on this credit, so the derived answer can be too generous and cannot be too mean, and the credit line SAYS SO in its own name whenever the staircase has not already settled it at zero. Pass `kentuckyModifiedGrossIncome` for the worksheet's own figure. The leading open model does not model line (c) either — its own comment says so — and does model line (d).

THE FAMILY SIZE COUNTED HERE IS ONE PERSON TOO LARGE FOR A FILER WITH A DEPENDENT WHO IS NOT A CHILD. KRS 141.066(1)(d) counts the taxpayer, the spouse and the taxpayer's QUALIFYING CHILDREN; this package is given `dependents` and nothing finer, so a dependent parent counts here and does not count in Kentucky. It runs the generous way — a threshold one person too large makes the ratio too small, the step too high and the tax too low — and it is the same gap Maryland's childless earned-income schedule and Wisconsin's match carry. It cannot bite above family size four, where the cap has already stopped counting.

UNRESOLVED — whether a Kentucky filer on a SEPARATE return may claim the $40 age credit for a spouse who has no gross income and is nobody's dependent. This is the IRC § 151(b) question this package tracks as `separateReturnSpouse` for four states' exemptions, and KRS 141.020(3) does not resolve from this sandbox to answer it. This package claims ONE credit on such a return and the reference model claims TWO, which is $40 on the differential grid's own household — a filer and spouse both 68 with $55,000 of pension. Charging the higher figure is the direction that cannot pay one household's credit twice; a caller who knows the answer can supply the other $40 through `subtractions` grossed up by the rate.

The combined-separate election is still not modelled and `tools/anchors` prices it at twenty cents. The note above has said since Day 8 that Form 740 filing status 2 is worth "about $131 of tax in 2025"; the anchored two-earner household at $60,000 and $40,000 is overstated by $130.80, and a second anchored household by $59.56.

A CORRECTION WORTH KEEPING, because this package published the wrong cause for two days and the upstream fixture it came from still carries it. The anchored Kentucky household with $400 and $31,429 was overstated by $551.18 — and the note here said $591.18, which was the figure from BEFORE the $40 age credit shipped — and both the fixture's own label and this package's note attributed the gap to the combined-separate election "preserving the age-65 credit against the column that can use it". It was not the election. It was the family size tax credit, which that household claims at 50% of its bill, and with the credit computed this package reproduces the expected $551.18 TO THE CENT with the election still unmodelled. The election costs that household nothing at all.

THE GENERAL LESSON, because it is the reason the correction above is in the shipped notes rather than only in a journal: A DISAGREEMENT CARRIES A NUMBER THAT CAN BE MEASURED AND A CAUSE THAT CANNOT, and the cause is the half a reader will act on. The fixture's label, this package's note and the figure in it were produced by three different runs and only the figure was ever re-derived. Two anchored Kentucky households remain overstated and their stated cause is the election; it is the best available reading and it is a reading, which is the part the $551.18 household is here to remember.

7 figures were supplied and spent on nothing: `federalDeductions`, `spouseAge`, `socialSecurityAndMedicarePaid`, `dependents`, `dependentAges`, `earnedIncome`, `retirement`. Every figure in this result — and every other note in it — is identical to the one this return would have had without them. That is MEASURED rather than looked up: the 2025 Kentucky return was computed again without each field and the answers compared. It does NOT mean Kentucky has no rule that reads the field, because a rule can need two fields together and the other one may be the one that is missing — Ohio reads `earnedIncome` only once `city` is supplied as well. It means nothing on THIS return moved, so a caller who went and looked the figures up bought no change in the answer by it.

credits.name: New Mexico working families tax credit (§ 7-2-18.15)
New Mexico child income tax credit (§ 7-2-18.34)
New Mexico low income comprehensive tax rebate (§ 7-2-14)

notes: NEW MEXICO'S $4,000 DEPENDENT DEDUCTION PAYS NOTHING FOR AN ONLY CHILD, AND EVERY PUBLISHED ACCOUNT OF IT OVERSTATES IT BY EXACTLY $4,000 FOR EVERY FAMILY OF EVERY SIZE. NMSA 1978 § 7-2-39 allows the deduction "for each dependent in excess of one": one child is $0, two are $4,000, four are $12,000. A model that pays $4,000 a dependent understates New Mexico tax by $172.00 in the 4.3% band, $188.00 at 4.7%, $196.00 at 4.9% and $236.00 at 5.9%, at every family size — which is the Arkansas property, a single number a buyer can check against one household and then trust for all of them. The design is legible once the count is right: HB 6 of 2019 created the deduction to offset the federal personal exemption that the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act set to zero, and New Mexico's deduction IS the federal standard deduction, which that Act had nearly doubled. The first dependent is the one the larger standard deduction was taken to cover.

A NEW MEXICO HEAD OF HOUSEHOLD IS TAXED ON THE MARRIED-COUPLE SCHEDULE, AND SO IS A SURVIVING SPOUSE. NMSA 1978 § 7-2-7 writes THREE schedules and not five: one for married individuals filing separately, one for single individuals, and one for married individuals filing joint returns, SURVIVING SPOUSES AND HEADS OF HOUSEHOLD. The Department's own rate table prints the joint column with the note that it "must also be used by surviving spouse" and gives head of household the same figures. A model that defaults a head of household to the single column overcharges by $202.00 at $66,500 of net taxable income, $269.00 from $100,000 to $210,000 and A FLAT $1,319.00 AT EVERY NET TAXABLE INCOME ABOVE $315,000 — the jump being the single column's 5.9% band opening $105,000 earlier than the joint one. The separate schedule is exactly half the joint one at every threshold, which test/new-mexico.test.js asserts.

NEW MEXICO'S SOCIAL SECURITY EXEMPTION IS A CLIFF AND IT IS IN FORCE. § 7-2-5.14 exempts the whole federally taxable benefit where federal AGI does not exceed $100,000 single, $150,000 joint, head of household or surviving spouse, or $75,000 married filing separately — with NO taper. A couple with $60,000 of federally taxable benefit pays nothing on it at $150,000 of AGI and $2,855.65 at $150,001; with $85,000 of benefit it is $3,961.85, and a single filer with $40,000 of benefit pays $1,914.85 for one dollar above $100,000. It is the largest LIVE discontinuity this package carries on a Social Security threshold, and test/new-mexico.test.js measures that over every state here rather than asserting it: Kansas charged $2,845.80 on the same shape at $75,000 and repealed it for tax year 2024, and Connecticut's surviving threshold is $405 for a couple with $40,000 of benefits. It is not the largest discontinuity in this package — Maryland's capital-gains surtax tests federal AGI against $350,000 rather than taking an excess, and one dollar there can cost $6,933.08.

THE THREE SOCIAL SECURITY THRESHOLDS ARE NOT INDEXED, ALTHOUGH A PUBLISHED 2026 GUIDE SAYS THEY ARE. HB 249 of the 2024 regular session would have adjusted all three for inflation from tax year 2025; it was POSTPONED INDEFINITELY ON 6 FEBRUARY 2024 and never became law. The 2025 PIT-ADJ instructions print the unindexed figures in their Table 2, and policyengine-us 2.87.0 carries all three from 2022-01-01 with no later value. A guide reaching this sandbox states the opposite — that HB 249 amended § 7-2-5.14 so that the base amounts are adjusted for inflation and rounded down to the nearest $100 — and on a cliff that is not a rounding difference: it moves the point at which an entire benefit becomes taxable, so a couple between $150,000 and an indexed figure is told they owe nothing on a benefit New Mexico taxes in full. This is the second consecutive state added here to carry an indexing clause that exists only in a bill or a fiscal note: Kansas's SB 1 as introduced would have indexed the standard deduction from 2025 and the enacted act does not.

THE LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME EXEMPTION IS $2,500 PER EXEMPTION AND NOT $2,500 A RETURN. § 7-2-5.8 multiplies the figure by the number of federal exemptions — filers plus dependents — so a joint return with two children claims four of them and $10,000 of exemption before the taper, which at 4.3% is $430.00 of tax. The taper is 10% of federal AGI above $30,000 joint, head of household and surviving spouse, 15% above $20,000 single, 20% above $15,000 separate. A SURVIVING SPOUSE COUNTS AS ONE EXEMPTION AND NOT TWO here, because § 151 allowed a qualifying widow(er) one personal exemption: the spouse is dead. That distinction doubled five states' allowances for a widow before v0.24.0 and this is the first new rule since to need it.

THE INCOME LIMIT ON THE LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME EXEMPTION CANNOT CHANGE ANYBODY'S TAX, WHICH IS WHY test/new-mexico.test.js ASSERTS IT RATHER THAN RELYING ON IT. The statute prints a limit of $55,000 joint, $36,667 single and $27,500 separate, and each is exactly where its own taper reaches zero: 30,000 + 2,500/0.10 = 55,000.00, 20,000 + 2,500/0.15 = 36,666.67, 15,000 + 2,500/0.20 = 27,500.00. So the limit can zero a positive exemption in no household, in any status, at any income. THE SINGLE ROW IS A THIRD OF A DOLLAR WIDE AND THE INDEPENDENT REFERENCE MODEL FALLS INTO IT: this package clamps the per-exemption amount at zero and that model does not, so for single AGI between $36,666.67 and $36,667 it computes 2,500 - 0.15 x 16,667 = -$0.05 an exemption and ADDS it to taxable income. Five cents on a four-person return, recorded for the shape and not the amount — a clamp omitted where two published figures were believed to coincide exactly.

THE AGED-OR-BLIND EXEMPTION HAS NOT BEEN INDEXED SINCE 1987 AND IT IS NINE CLIFFS, NOT A TAPER. § 7-2-5.2 gives up to $8,000 to each person 65 or over or blind, falling in whole $1,000 steps: single $8,000 to $18,000 of AGI then a step every $1,500 and nothing from $28,500; joint and head of household $8,000 to $30,000 then every $3,000 and nothing from $51,000; separate $8,000 to $15,000 then every $1,500 and nothing from $25,500. One dollar of AGI at a boundary costs the whole $1,000 of allowance AND MOST OF THE STEPS ARE STILL FREE: measured for 2026, four of the eight single boundaries cost nothing and the other four cost $14.27, $15.01, $30.34 and $32.04, because the exemption expires at $28,500 of AGI and a single New Mexican there has $8,125 of taxable income — inside the 3.2% band, so nobody who reaches 4.3% still holds the exemption. The largest step in the state is $64.04, at the joint $51,000 boundary, where both people's exemptions fall on the same dollar. Pricing these steps at the state's top rates is the mistake the first draft of this module made, and the measurement is what caught it. The thresholds are the 1987 figures on the reference model's parameter files, which carry every one of them from 1987-01-01 with no later value; the separate table is NOT half the joint one, unlike the rate schedule.

AGED AND BLIND DO NOT STACK ON ONE PERSON IN NEW MEXICO, WHICH IS THE OPPOSITE OF FEDERAL § 63(f). § 7-2-5.2 reaches a person "sixty-five years of age or older OR blind", so a single New Mexican who is both gets $8,000 once and not twice. Kansas's Worksheet I gives such a filer two boxes at $850 each, the federal standard deduction gives two additions of $2,050, and every state addition in this package modelled on § 63(f) stacks them. New Mexico is the first state here where the two conditions are alternatives.

ONLY THE AGE HALF OF THE AGED-OR-BLIND EXEMPTION IS COMPUTED HERE, AND A BLIND NEW MEXICAN UNDER 65 IS CHARGED TOO MUCH BY UP TO $8,000 OF EXEMPTION, and the cost is bounded by the income at which the exemption survives rather than by the state's top rate: a single filer still holding the whole $8,000 has AGI of $18,000 or less, where the federal deduction has already taken the tax to zero, so the omission is worth nothing at all for most of the band it covers and at most a few tens of dollars anywhere in it. That is the same measurement that priced the staircase above, applied to an omission. The obstacle is the input and not the statute: the one field in this package that carries blindness is `blindOrDisabled`, which is New Jersey's and counts a filer who is "blind or permanently disabled", where § 7-2-5.2 reaches blindness alone and the field does not say which person on a joint return is which. Reading it would grant the exemption to a disabled New Mexican the subsection does not reach, so it is not read — the same decision, for the same reason, as Kansas's disabled-veteran exemption. Supply it through `subtractions` as the table amount for the status and AGI.

NEW MEXICO'S DEDUCTION IS THE FEDERAL ONE, SO THE ONE BIG BEAUTIFUL BILL ACT CUT NEW MEXICO TAX WITH NO NEW MEXICO LEGISLATION. PIT-1 line 12 is "Federal standard or itemized deduction amount (from federal Form 1040, line 12)" and the state legislates no deduction of its own and no personal exemption at all. A single New Mexican's deduction was $15,000 under the pre-Act schedule and is $15,750 for 2025 and $16,100 for 2026; a joint return's is $32,200 for 2026. At 4.9% the 2026 increase alone is worth $53.90 single and $107.80 joint against the figures a model built before July 2025 carries. AND THE § 63(f) ADDITION FOR AGE AND BLINDNESS REACHES A NEW MEXICO RETURN TOO, because line 12 is the deduction the filer ACTUALLY TOOK: $2,050 for a single filer 65 or over in 2026, $1,650 each on a joint return. That is Missouri's answer and not Arizona's — Arizona's statute sets its deduction equal to the federal standard AMOUNT in a flat table, so the addition does not reach an Arizona return, and this package was wrong about Arizona for 47 days for exactly that reason. A NEW MEXICO RETIREE THEREFORE COLLECTS AN AGE ALLOWANCE TWICE, once inside line 12 and again under § 7-2-5.2, which is a fact about two provisions rather than a double-count here.

NEW MEXICO TAXES TIPS AND OVERTIME THAT THE FEDERAL GOVERNMENT NOW EXEMPTS. PIT-1 line 9 is federal adjusted gross income and all four OBBBA Schedule 1-A deductions — § 224 tips, § 225 overtime, § 151(d)(5) senior and § 163(h)(4) vehicle loan interest — sit BELOW it, so none of them reaches the New Mexico base and New Mexico has legislated no subtraction of its own for any of them. A tipped New Mexico worker with $8,000 of qualified tips and $50,000 of AGI pays $345.60 of state tax on income the federal return exempted entirely — measured, because the $8,000 straddles the 4.3% and 4.7% bands — rising to $472.00 where the dollars fall wholly in the 5.9% band. The senior deduction is the sharpest of the four here, because New Mexico already has two age allowances of its own and this third one does not arrive.

THE 40% CAPITAL GAINS DEDUCTION IS GONE FOR EVERYBODY WHO DID NOT SELL A NEW MEXICO BUSINESS. § 7-2-34 allowed the greater of $1,000 or 40% of net capital gain through tax year 2024; HB 252 of 2024 restricted the 40% element to the gain from the sale of a New Mexico business and raised the flat element to $2,500, from tax year 2025. So the deduction an ordinary filer gets is min(net capital gain, $2,500), worth $122.50 at 4.9%, against $9,800 on a $200,000 gain under the repealed percentage. Several published accounts of this state still describe the 40% deduction as current for everybody, which understates the tax on that gain by $4,011.50: a single New Mexican with a $200,000 long-term gain and $250,000 of AGI owes $11,010.60 for 2026 and $6,999.10 under the repealed 40%, because the $77,500 of difference comes out of the 5.9% and 4.9% bands. THE BUSINESS-SALE ELEMENT IS NOT MODELLED — no field here records what was sold or where — so a New Mexico answer computed here is too HIGH for such a seller.

THE CHILD INCOME TAX CREDIT IS MODELLED FROM THE DEPARTMENT'S OWN TABLE, AND THE BAND EDGES ARE THE PART A MODEL GETS WRONG. § 7-2-18.34 pays a REFUNDABLE credit per qualifying child, read against federal AGI from PIT-1 line 9: $637 to $25,000, then $424, $212, $106, $79, $53 and $26, halved on a married-filing-separate return. TABLE 4 ON PAGE RC-11 OF THE 2025 PIT-RC INSTRUCTIONS PRINTS THE BANDS WITH A "BUT NOT OVER" COLUMN — $0–25,000, 25,001–50,000, 50,001–75,000, 75,001–100,000, 100,001–200,000, 200,001–350,000, 350,001 and over — so every round figure is the TOP of its band and the next band opens one dollar later. A model that stores the left column as a lower bound pays one band too little at all six edges: $424 instead of $637 at exactly $25,000 and $212 instead of $424 at $50,000, which is a quarter of the credit. The six cliffs are $213, $212, $106, $27, $26 and $27 a child, every one measured. The independent reference model stores the left column and corrects with a right=True scale lookup, which is right at five edges and wrong at the sixth, because its own threshold is written 75,001 where the other five are round: a filer at exactly $75,001 of AGI is paid $212 there where the table says $106. The credit runs for taxable years beginning on or after 1 January 2023 and before 1 January 2032 for a resident who is not a dependent of another individual, and the amounts are ONE OF THE TWO SETS OF INDEXED FIGURES IN THE NEW MEXICO INCOME TAX — the other is § 7-2-14's rebate table — so 2026 carries 2025's figures forward and says so.

§ 152(c) IS NOT § 32'S QUALIFYING CHILD, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS AN ITIN. § 7-2-18.34(J)(2) defines "qualifying child" as IRC § 152(c)'s, and the 2025 PIT-RC instructions print the definition in full and EXPAND it — it "includes any minor child or stepchild of the taxpayer who would be a qualifying child for federal income tax purposes if the public assistance contributing to the support of the child or stepchild was considered to have been contributed by the taxpayer". § 152(c) CARRIES NO IDENTIFICATION-NUMBER REQUIREMENT; § 32(m) does, denying the federal earned income credit without a Social Security number valid for work. So a New Mexico child with an ITIN is a qualifying child for this credit and is not one for the federal credit, and the independent reference model counts eitc_child_count here — its own comment says "IRC 152(c) refers to the EITC qualifying children", which is the conflation. That model therefore denies the WHOLE $637 a child to such a family. WHAT THIS PACKAGE CANNOT SEE IS THE OTHER TWO LIMBS OF § 152(c)(3): a STUDENT under 24 and a permanently and totally disabled child of ANY age both qualify, and only the under-19 test is applied here, so a family with either is understated by the whole per-child amount and its New Mexico tax overstated. The obstacle is the input and not the statute — nothing here records that a dependent is a student or disabled. Supply the amount yourself through `subtractions` as a negative, or read `credits` and add to it. AND WITH NO `dependentAges` THE CREDIT IS ZERO, deliberately: a count of dependents does not say they are children, and guessing the generous way would turn a missing input into a refundable credit.

NEW MEXICO'S OWN RATE TABLE COMPUTES $2.00 LESS THAN NEW MEXICO'S OWN RATE SCHEDULE, AT EVERY TAXABLE INCOME ABOVE $100,000, FOREVER — AND THIS PACKAGE COMPUTES THE SCHEDULE. The 2025 TAX RATE TABLE on pages T-1 to T-6 of the PIT packet is a $100-WIDE MIDPOINT table: the row for $99,900–$100,000 prints $4,356 for a single filer, which is the exact § 7-2-7 tax at $99,950 rounded to the dollar, and the exact tax at $100,000 is $4,358.00. The continuation table for incomes over $100,000 then uses the MIDPOINT FIGURE as its base — "Single, not over $210,000: your tax is $4,356 plus 4.9% of taxable income in excess of $100,000" — so the Department's prescribed computation sits $2.00 below the statutory schedule at every income above the breakpoint and never converges, because both run at the same marginal rates from there. It is $2.00 for a single filer, a joint return and a head of household ($4,087 printed against $4,089.00 exact) and $2.50 for a married filer filing separately ($4,492 against $4,494.50). THIS PACKAGE RETURNS THE SCHEDULE because § 7-2-7 is the law and the table is an aid the Department publishes, so a New Mexico answer here is $2.00 ABOVE what the form a filer actually submits will show. BELOW $100,000 the table is a midpoint table too, so a filed return differs from the schedule by up to about $2.45 either way — half a $100 band at 4.9% — depending where in its row the income falls. test/new-mexico.test.js pins the four printed bases, the midpoint derivation and the constancy of the gap. It is the only figure in this package measured against a STATE FORM rather than against a statute or another model.

THE 2025 PIT PACKET WAS READ, WHICH IS THE FIRST PRIMARY NEW MEXICO DOCUMENT THIS PACKAGE HAS OPENED, AND IT SETTLED FOUR THINGS THAT HAD BEEN INFERENCES. Seventeen consecutive runs recorded every New Mexico host as unreachable and they still are — tax.newmexico.gov, realfile.tax.newmexico.gov, nmlegis.gov, nmonesource.com and law.justia.com all fail to resolve — but the file host the Department serves its own packet from does not. (1) THE LINE 13 WORKSHEET SAYS "Subtract 1 from total dependents" in terms, so the $4,000 dependent deduction paying nothing for an only child is now a reading of the Department's own worksheet and not of three secondary records. (2) THE LINE 5 WORKSHEET COUNTS THE SPOUSE ONLY "if married filing jointly", which settles whether a separate return may count the IRC § 151(b) spouse among its "federal exemptions" for § 7-2-5.8: it may not, which is what this package already computed. (3) LINE 13'S INSTRUCTION NAMES "a head of household or married filing jointly" AND NOT A SURVIVING SPOUSE, while LINE 14 on the facing page names "married filing jointly, surviving spouse, or head of household" — two instructions a page apart, one grouping her in and the other leaving her out, which is the strongest evidence available for the literal reading that gives her no dependent deduction. (4) PIT-ADJ TABLE 2 PRINTS THE UNINDEXED SOCIAL SECURITY THRESHOLDS of $100,000, $75,000 and $150,000, against the published 2026 guide that asserts HB 249's indexation passed. The PIT-TRT pages also print the joint column with the footnote "This column must also be used by surviving spouse" and give head of household the same figures.

THE LOW INCOME COMPREHENSIVE TAX REBATE IS MODELLED FROM THE DEPARTMENT'S OWN TABLE 1, AND THE TABLE IS NOT MONOTONIC IN INCOME. § 7-2-14 pays a REFUNDABLE rebate read out of a grid of 23 modified-gross-income bands by six exemption columns, 138 cells, allowed only where modified gross income is $36,000 or less, and halved on a separate return. IT IS THE ONLY AMOUNT IN THIS PACKAGE THAT RISES WITH INCOME: the $0–$1,000 row is BELOW the $1,001–$1,500 row in every one of the six columns, so the dollar that takes a filer from $1,000 to $1,001 of modified gross income is worth $28 to a one-exemption household and $178 to a six-exemption one. The column maxima are not even in the same row — columns 1 to 4 peak at $1,001–$7,500, column 5 at $7,501–$9,000 and column 6 at $2,501–$8,000 — so the table is six schedules and not one profile scaled six ways, which is why all 138 cells are written out rather than generated. The largest single payment is $839 and the smallest is $17.

THE REBATE IS BANDED ON MODIFIED GROSS INCOME, WHICH IS NEITHER FEDERAL AGI NOR NEW MEXICO TAXABLE INCOME, AND IT IS THE BROADEST INCOME DEFINITION ON THE RETURN. PIT-RC lines 4 to 11 build it out of eight GROSS figures and the form states the relationship itself — the total "must equal or exceed Federal Adjusted Gross Income from Form PIT-1, line 9". It takes the WHOLE Social Security benefit rather than the part IRC § 86 makes taxable, and adds public assistance, TANF, SSI, gifts of cash or marketable items received, scholarships, grants, insurance settlements, trust income, inheritance and child support; it floors net business, farm and rental losses at zero and refuses to net capital losses against capital gains, which N.M. Admin. Code § 3.3.1.10 states in terms — "zero is the lowest amount which may be reported for any item". SO A REBATE AIMED AT THE POOREST HOUSEHOLDS IS MEANS-TESTED ON THE WIDEST INCOME IN THE STATE, which is the opposite of what the rest of the New Mexico return does. PASS IT AS `newMexicoModifiedGrossIncome`. Without it the engine derives a FLOOR — federal AGI, plus tax-exempt interest, plus the untaxed part of any Social Security benefit given through `retirement` — and names the assumption on the credit line, because a floor on the income is a CEILING on the rebate. The Social Security term is the one that moves households: a couple on $24,000 of benefit and $12,000 of pension has $12,000 of federal AGI if § 86 taxes none of the benefit and $36,000 of modified gross income, which is a $655 rebate read on AGI and a $40 one read on the floor.

THE EXEMPTION COUNT THE REBATE'S COLUMN IS CHOSEN BY IS NOT THE EXEMPTION COUNT, AND AGE IS WORTH TWICE WHAT BLINDNESS IS. PIT-RC line 2 builds its own: federal exemptions, plus TWO for each filer 65 or over (lines 2e and 2f) and ONE for each blind filer (line 2c). That is the reverse of IRC § 63(f), where the age and blindness additions are equal and stack on one person, and the reverse again of New Mexico's own § 7-2-5.2, where the two conditions are ALTERNATIVES and a person who is both qualifies once — three provisions, three different weightings, all on the same two facts about the same filer. A single New Mexican of 65 is therefore a THREE-exemption household on Table 1 and a couple both 65 is a SIX-exemption one, reading the last column that a family of six reads: $839 at $2,501–$7,500 of modified gross income for 2025, where their federal return knows of two people. TWO SUBTRACTIONS ON THE SAME PAGE ARE NOT MODELLED, and both make this count an upper bound and the rebate a ceiling: line 2a removes household members who do not qualify, and line 2h removes, on a separate return, the exemptions the other spouse claimed on THEIR PIT-RC — a figure that exists only on a different return. The blindness count is read from `blindOrDisabled`, which is New Jersey's field and counts a filer who is "blind or permanently disabled", where line 2c reaches blindness alone: a disabled New Mexican who is not blind is given one exemption too many, worth at most one column of the table.

THE REBATE'S 138 AMOUNTS ARE INDEXED, THE INDEXATION IS CUMULATIVE RATHER THAN CHAINED, AND THE DEPARTMENT CHANGED ITS ROUNDING RULE AFTER 2023 — ALL THREE ESTABLISHED FROM FIVE PUBLISHED TABLES AND NOT FROM THE STATUTE. The 2021 and 2022 packets print the same table cell for cell and it is the statutory base; 2023, 2024 and 2025 are that base scaled by ONE cumulative factor each. CHAINING IS ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE: no single factor takes the 2023 table to the 2024 one, or the 2024 table to the 2025 one, under truncation or under round-half-up, so a model that uprates last year's PUBLISHED figures cannot reproduce what New Mexico prints however good its index is. AND THE ROUNDING RULE IS NOT CONSTANT: round-half-up reproduces all 138 cells of the 2023 table and truncation reproduces at most 100 of them; truncation reproduces all 138 of 2024 and all 138 of 2025 and round-half-up reproduces at most 93 and 98. Each rules the other out by dozens of cells, so neither is a typo. The realised cumulative factors against the 2021 base lie in [1.0820000, 1.0820225) for 2023, [1.1220339, 1.1222222) for 2024 and [1.1493333, 1.1494505) for 2025; none of the three contains the CPI-U annual-average ratio to 2021, so THE INDEX IS NOT IDENTIFIED and this package does not project 2026 from it. 2026 carries 2025 forward in 23 provisionalFigures entries on the AMOUNTS only — not on the bands, which have been identical in all five tables. The leading open model stores the same published cells and uprates them with the federal C-CPI-U and a `rounding: nearest` rule, which is the rule New Mexico stopped using after 2023.

THE REBATE'S FOUR ELIGIBILITY CONDITIONS ARE NOT TESTED HERE AND ALL FOUR WOULD REDUCE THE REBATE, NEVER RAISE IT. PIT-RC Section 1 requires that the claimant was a New Mexico resident during the year, was physically present in New Mexico for at least six months, was NOT eligible to be claimed as a dependent of another taxpayer, and was NOT an inmate of a public institution for more than six months. Nothing in this package's inputs records any of them, so a rebate computed here is paid to a claimant the Department would refuse — most commonly a student or young adult who is somebody else's dependent, for whom the whole rebate is wrong and not part of it. The independent reference model does not test them either. Residence is the one the rest of this package already assumes everywhere, and the dependent condition is the one worth passing on to a caller: if the filer is claimed on another return, subtract the whole rebate.

NOT MODELLED — THE OTHER FOUR REFUNDABLE ITEMS ON PIT-RC, and each would further reduce a low-income New Mexico return computed here. The property tax rebate for persons 65 or older (Section 3, up to $250, needing property tax billed or rent paid and the Table 2 maximum-liability schedule); the ADDITIONAL low income property tax rebate (Section 4, up to $350, LOS ALAMOS, SANTA FE, DOÑA ANA AND BERNALILLO COUNTIES ONLY, needing a county this package does not carry for New Mexico because no New Mexico locality levies an income tax); the child day care credit of § 7-2-18.1 (Section 5, up to $1,200, needing day care expense and the federal credit actually applied); and the refundable medical care credit for persons 65 or older. All four are gated on the same modified gross income figure Section 2 uses, at $16,000, $24,000, $30,160 and their own limits.

A SURVIVING SPOUSE GETS THE JOINT RATE SCHEDULE AND NO DEPENDENT DEDUCTION, AND THE SECOND HALF IS THE CONTESTABLE READING. New Mexico's PIT-1 carries five filing-status boxes including "Surviving Spouse with dependent child"; § 7-2-7 sends her to the married-filing-jointly schedule by name; and § 7-2-39 allows its $4,000 to a return filed "as a head of household or married filing jointly" and names no other status. This package takes the literal reading, which is also the independent reference model's, and the cost of being wrong is $4,000 of deduction on a widow with two children: $188.00 of tax on $90,000 of AGI, measured, and $172.00 to $236.00 elsewhere depending on the band the deduction comes out of. The reading that cannot be settled from this sandbox is whether a New Mexico surviving spouse "files a return as ... married filing jointly" for the purposes of § 7-2-39 when the state gives her a box of her own; the 2025 PIT-1 instructions group the three statuses together in several other places, which is the best argument for the other side. If the other reading is right, add $4,000 per dependent after the first through `subtractions` for a widow.

THE ARMED FORCES RETIREMENT PAY EXEMPTION IS SCHEDULED TO END AFTER TAX YEAR 2026, AND THE INDEPENDENT REFERENCE MODEL DOES NOT KNOW IT. § 7-2-5.13 exempts $30,000 per military retiree and per surviving spouse of one, with no age test, no income test and no cap beyond the figure — $10,000 for 2022, $20,000 for 2023, $30,000 from 2024 — and the enacted provision runs through tax year 2026 only. SB 56 and SB 125 of 2024 would have removed the sunset and HB 221 of 2026 would have made the exemption total; none is recorded here as enacted. BOTH YEARS THIS MODULE COVERS ARE INSIDE THE WINDOW, so the sunset changes no answer here, and it is written down because it changes one in 2027: policyengine-us 2.87.0 carries the $30,000 from 2024-01-01 with no end date and so exempts the pay indefinitely, which would understate a 2027 New Mexico return by up to $1,770.00 at 5.9%.

NEW MEXICO ITEMIZED DEDUCTIONS ARE NOT READ HERE, AND THE ELECTION IS LOCKED TO THE FEDERAL ONE. PIT-1 line 12 takes whichever figure the filer used federally, so a New Mexico filer who itemized federally must itemize in New Mexico — the trap Oklahoma sets, and the opposite of Kansas, which lets a filer choose whichever is better. `stateItemizedDeductions` is ignored for New Mexico and an itemiser is computed on the figure passed in `federal.deduction`, which is the right answer when that field carries the deduction actually taken. New Mexico also adds back the part of the federal state-and-local tax deduction attributable to its own income tax for an itemiser, which is not modelled: an itemising New Mexico return computed here is too LOW by that amount.

NO CITY, COUNTY OR SCHOOL DISTRICT IN NEW MEXICO LEVIES AN INCOME TAX. The state figure is the whole of a New Mexico resident's income tax, so `locality` is never required and `SUPPORTED_LOCALITIES` names none here.

NOT MODELLED, AND EACH WOULD REDUCE A NEW MEXICO RETURN COMPUTED HERE: the $2,500 exemption under § 7-2-5.7 for a person ONE HUNDRED YEARS OF AGE OR OLDER, which exempts all of their income and which this package has no household shape to reach usefully; the unreimbursed medical care expense exemption and credit of § 7-2-5.11 and § 7-2-18.30, each needing a medical expense figure no input carries; the New Mexico 529 contribution deduction; the credit for taxes paid to another state; and the medical care expense DEDUCTION of § 7-2-37, whose three rates were reduced to ZERO from tax year 2025 and so is correctly absent from both years here rather than omitted.

Two wage earner credit (assumed: one earner — pass lesserSpouseIncome, worth up to $350)

notes: The starting point for 2025 is FEDERAL TAXABLE INCOME, so a 2025 South Carolina return inherits the federal standard or itemized deduction — and then takes part of it back. South Carolina conforms to the Internal Revenue Code only as amended through 31 DECEMBER 2024 (§ 12-6-40(A)(1)(a)), and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act was enacted 4 July 2025, so the Act’s increase in the standard deduction and all four of its Schedule 1-A deductions — tips, overtime, the senior deduction and vehicle loan interest — are added back. South Carolina does NOT allow the federal § 199A qualified business income deduction: § 12-6-50 names it among the federal provisions the state does not adopt. This package adds it back automatically when you pass `federalDeductions.qualifiedBusinessIncome`.

SOUTH CAROLINA TAXES EVERY FILING STATUS ON THE SAME RATE SCHEDULE. The brackets do not widen on a joint return, in either year, which is a fact about the statute (§ 12-6-510) and not an omission here — and it is the whole of South Carolina’s marriage penalty, because everything else on the return scales. In 2025 a couple at $120,000 pay $4,758.30 against $4,116.60 for two single filers at $60,000 each: $641.70, which is exactly what the graduated schedule is worth to one filer ($3,560 at 6% plus $14,270 at 3%), so the couple lose one filer’s whole schedule. In 2026 the penalty is $965.99 and is the SAME NUMBER SCDOR PRINTS ON THE RATE SCHEDULE: the $966 of "5.21% minus $966" is $30,000 x (5.21% - 1.99%), and a couple who do not get a second $30,000 band pay exactly that. The reported figure is a cent light because the single return’s own tax carries a half-cent that rounds up, twice — the difference of the answers as reported, not of the figures behind them. Virginia is the only other state in this package that does not widen its brackets.
South Carolina does not tax Social Security benefits at all: the federally taxable amount is subtracted in full, at any age and any income. Pass `taxableSocialSecurity`.

THE $15,000 SENIOR DEDUCTION IS AN AGE PROVISION AND NOT A RETIREMENT ONE, and every guide files it under retirement income. § 12-6-1170(B) allows a filer of 65 to deduct $15,000 of ANY income, reduced by whatever that person deducted under subsection (A) — so the pair is a FLOOR of $15,000 rather than $15,000 on top of the retirement deduction. A single South Carolina filer of 66 with $60,000 pays $1,038.30 whether that $60,000 is pension or wages, and the same person at 50 with the same pension pays $1,878.30, because the retirement deduction alone is $3,000 under 65. The $840.00 difference is deduction and not income, and it is $14,000 of it at 6%: $12,000 from the $15,000 floor against the $3,000 cap, and $2,000 that is not a South Carolina provision at all — IRC § 63(f)’s additional standard deduction for a filer who has attained 65, which the frozen Code allows in full and which the standard deduction add-back must not reach. Through v0.46.0 it did, and every South Carolina filer of 65 or over was taxed on that $2,000: $120 of tax, in the direction nobody complains about.

MILITARY RETIRED PAY IS DEDUCTED IN FULL, AT ANY AGE, WITH NO CAP — § 12-6-1171, the Workforce Enhancement and Military Recognition Act of 2022. A single filer with $60,000 of military retired pay and nothing else owes South Carolina NOTHING, at 50 and at 66 alike, where the same $60,000 of civilian government pension costs $1,878.30 at 50. Pass it as `retirement.filer.militaryRetirement`, not through `retirementIncome`, which cannot tell the two apart.

AND IT IS DEDUCTED IN FULL OUT OF A SHARED CAP, WHICH IS THE PART EVERY SUMMARY OF § 12-6-1171 LEAVES OUT. § 12-6-1170(C)(1) reduces the deduction allowed by THAT WHOLE SECTION — (A)’s $3,000/$10,000 general retirement deduction as well as (B)’s $15,000 senior deduction — by whatever is deducted under § 12-6-1171, and the 2025 SC1040 instructions apply it on line 3 of the line p-1 and p-2 worksheets, before the retirement-income limit. So a military retiree’s OTHER retirement income is deducted at $0 and not at $10,000: a 65-year-old with $60,000 of retired pay and a $20,000 civilian pension subtracts $60,000, not $70,000. The two rules compose into a FLOOR rather than a sum — at 65 the total is max($15,000, military + min(other, max($0, $10,000 − military))) — so below $5,000 of retired pay the senior deduction fills the hole and the answer is unchanged, and from $20,000 of it the whole $10,000 is gone. Worth $600 of 2025 tax and $521 of 2026 tax at the top rate. This package had it wrong until v0.45.0, and in the taxpayer’s favour, which is the direction a filer hears about from the Department rather than from their software.

THE SURVIVING SPOUSE CLAIMS BOTH DEDUCTIONS A SECOND TIME, AND THE DECEASED SPOUSE KEEPS AGEING. A surviving spouse who receives qualified retirement income on a deceased spouse’s behalf deducts it on SC1040 line p-3 SEPARATELY from their own, and § 12-6-1170(A) allows it “in the same manner” the decedent would have taken it — so the $3,000/$10,000 cap is set by the age the DECEASED SPOUSE WOULD HAVE REACHED in the tax year and not by the claimant’s, which SCDOR states as a rule about time: the figure rises “for the year the deceased spouse would have been 65 and older”. The decedent’s military retired pay comes out in full under § 12-6-1171 on a line of its own. AND (C)(1) DOES NOT REACH EITHER OF THEM — the SC1040 instructions say “do not reduce the surviving spouse retirement deduction by any surviving spouse military retirement deduction taken”, and SCDOR says the age 65 and older deduction “is not reduced by any surviving spouse retirement deduction” — so the paragraph above runs the other way for a widow. A single filer of 65 whose husband would have been 70, with her own $20,000 civilian pension, his $30,000 of military retired pay and his $15,000 pension, deducts $55,000: her own $10,000, his $30,000, his $10,000, and the $5,000 of senior deduction her own cap leaves. Treating the same dollars as her own gives $30,000 — $25,000 less, $1,500.00 of 2025 tax and $1,302.50 of 2026 tax. Pass `survivorPension`, `survivorMilitaryRetirement` and `deceasedSpouseAge`; this package modelled none of it before v0.46.0 and was too HIGH for that household, which is the only South Carolina household it has ever been too high for.

ONE DECEASED SPOUSE IS MODELLED. The SC1040 instructions tell a filer claiming the surviving-spouse deduction for MORE THAN ONE deceased spouse to “calculate the deduction separately for each deceased spouse” and to attach a statement of each date of birth, so a survivor of two marriages has one $3,000/$10,000 cap per decedent and `deceasedSpouseAge` holds one age. Supply the largest decedent’s figures in the survivor fields and the remaining decedents’ deductions through `subtractions`.

The 44% net capital gain deduction (§ 12-6-1150) makes a long-term gain cost 2.9176% in 2026 against 5.21% on a wage, and 3.36% in 2025 against 6%. It is worth $2,292.40 on $100,000 of gain to a 2026 filer in the top band. The base is the IRC § 1222(11) "net capital gain", so a short-term LOSS eats the deduction and a short-term GAIN cannot create one: pass `netCapitalGain` (Form 1040 line 7) and `shortTermCapitalGains` to split it. Supplying only the net figure treats all of it as long-term, which is the most generous reading and the only one a single netted number supports.

Interest on obligations of the United States is exempt and is NOT modelled as a subtraction here — pass it through `subtractions`. The same goes for the South Carolina college investment (529) deduction and the subsistence allowance for police, firefighters and emergency personnel.

NOT MODELLED, and the largest gap for a business owner: the § 12-6-545 reduced rate on active trade or business income. South Carolina taxes income from a pass-through trade or business at a flat rate of its own rather than at the schedule rate, so a South Carolina return with Schedule C, partnership or S corporation income computed here is TOO HIGH by the rate differential on that income.

NOT MODELLED: the § 12-6-1130(2) add-back of state and local income taxes deducted on federal Schedule A. It needs the Schedule A detail — the itemized total, the standard deduction that was forgone, the SALT cap and the real estate taxes inside it — and this package does not ask for them. A South Carolina ITEMIZER computed here is too LOW. Supply the add-back through `additions`.

notes: Utah's statutory rate is not its marginal rate for most working filers. The Taxpayer Tax Credit is 6% of the federal standard or itemized deduction plus $2,111 per dependent, reduced by 1.3 cents for each dollar of Utah taxable income above $18,213 ($36,426 joint). Inside that band the true marginal rate is the statutory rate plus 1.3 points — 5.75% in 2026 against a headline 4.45%.

The credit depends on the FEDERAL deduction, so Utah is a federal-AGI state whose credit is nonetheless sensitive to changes below AGI. The OBBBA standard deduction increase raised the Utah credit by 6% of the increase — $45.00 for a single filer in 2025 and $90.00 for a joint one — cutting Utah tax with no Utah legislation. (This note said $69 until Day 46, which measured the increase from the 2024 standard deduction of $14,600 rather than from the $15,000 that Rev. Proc. 2024-40 had already set for 2025. The OBBBA increase is $750, not $1,150.)

AND UTAH IS THE ONLY STATE HERE WHERE THAT FEDERAL INCREASE IS WORTH NOTHING AT THE TOP. Arizona, Colorado, Idaho and Missouri read the federal deduction through their base or through a deduction of their own, so the benefit is the state rate times the increase at every income. Utah reads it through a credit that withdraws at 1.3 cents on the dollar, so the benefit is a BAND: a 2025 single filer taking the standard deduction keeps the full $45.00 to $87,444 of federal AGI, loses it progressively above that, and gets exactly $0.00 from $90,906 upwards. At the bottom it is capped too, because the credit is non-refundable — a filer at $20,000 gains $23.23 rather than $45.00, since the credit already covered more of their tax than the increase is worth.
Utah cut its rate twice in two years: 4.55% for 2024, 4.5% for 2025 (HB 106), and 4.45% for 2026 (SB 60).

Utah's child tax credit is withdrawn at TEN cents on the dollar — 2.2 times the state's own tax rate, so the withdrawal is a larger marginal tax than the tax is. $1,000 for each child under 6, gone by $59,000 of income for a single filer with one child and $71,000 for a couple ($49,000/$61,000 in 2026 after HB 290, $43,000/$54,000 in 2025). Inside the band a Utah family faces about 14.75% on the next dollar against a headline 4.45%, and 16.05% where the Taxpayer Tax Credit is being withdrawn at the same time.

The child tax credit is withdrawn against a DIFFERENT income figure from Utah's retirement credits, on the same return. TC-40 line 9 — state taxable income, after every Utah subtraction — plus tax-exempt interest, where the Retirement and Social Security Benefits credits use line 6, before them. A Utah subtraction therefore buys back child credit and does nothing for a retiree's.

The credit is per child under 6 and ends the year the child turns 6, so a Utah family loses $1,000 on a birthday and nothing on the return says why. HB 106 (2025) widened it from the 1-to-3 band it had in 2024, where a newborn did not qualify at all.
Not modelled: the Utah credits for at-home parents and 529 contributions. A family claiming either will compute too high here.

Utah's earned income credit is 20% of the federal credit and is NON-REFUNDABLE — Utah Code § 59-10-1044 sits in Part 10, the Nonrefundable Tax Credit Act. It is the only state credit in this package that is a share of the federal credit and cannot be paid out, and the difference is the whole point of the credit for the filers it is aimed at: a Utah single parent whose Taxpayer Tax Credit already wipes out their tax receives nothing from it.

Utah taxes Social Security and then hands the tax back. The Social Security Benefits Credit (code AH, § 59-10-1042) is the state's own rate applied to the part of the benefit § 86 made taxable, so below $90,000 of modified AGI ($54,000 single, $45,000 separate) the benefit costs a Utah retiree nothing — and above it the credit is withdrawn at 2.5 cents on the dollar. SB 71 (2025) raised those thresholds 20% from $75,000/$45,000/$37,500 and they are NOT indexed.

A retiree may claim only ONE side of Utah's retirement credits: the Retirement Credit (code 18) on one side, or the Social Security Benefits Credit (code AH) together with the Military Retirement Credit (code AJ) on the other — § 59-10-1019(5). This engine computes both sides and takes the larger, which is always optimal because a non-refundable credit is worth min(itself, tax remaining) and min is monotone. The result names the side that was taken.

Utah's real marginal rate on a retiree reaches 15.26% — 3.4 times the 4.45% statutory rate — and it is three rules compounding, none of which is a bracket. A dollar of pension drags 85 cents of Social Security into federal AGI under § 86; Utah taxes all $1.85 at 4.45%, withdraws 2.5 cents of AH per dollar of it and 1.3 cents of Taxpayer Tax Credit per dollar of it. 1.85 x 8.25%. For a couple with a $70,000 benefit the rate runs 10.64% -> 15.26% -> 8.25% as income rises, peaking at $90,387.50 of federal AGI and FALLING after it, so the highest-taxed next dollar in Utah belongs to a household in the 12% federal bracket.

Tax-exempt interest is added back for both credits (§ 59-10-1019(1)(b), § 59-10-1042(1)(b)), so a municipal bond is taxed at 2.5% in Utah while appearing on no line of Utah income. For a couple with $40,000 of benefits and $60,000 of pension, $10,000 of exempt interest costs exactly $250.00 of Utah tax and $0.00 of federal tax. Pass it as `taxExemptInterest`; leaving it out understates a bondholding retiree.

The Retirement Credit (code 18) is all but dead law and the arithmetic says so. Its $450 a head is withdrawn at 2.5 cents against thresholds of $25,000 single and $32,000 joint that have not moved since the credit was written, so it is gone by $42,900 of modified AGI for a single filer and $67,900 for a couple — and below about $45,300 the Taxpayer Tax Credit has already reduced the tax to zero, leaving nothing for it to offset. Its whole live band for a couple is $45,300 to $67,900 of modified AGI, where it is worth at most $395.00, and only for a household with no Social Security at all, because any benefit makes code AH the larger side. Utah's own guidance says as much.

Code 18 also has a closed birth cohort: only a filer born on or before 31 December 1952 qualifies, a date that has never moved, so the eligible population shrinks every year and the credit sunsets by attrition rather than by repeal. It is the third such provision in this package after Virginia's 1939 age deduction and Kentucky's 1998 service cutoff. In 2026 it reaches a couple aged 74 and over: at $50,000 of modified AGI a couple born in 1951 pays $0.00 and the same couple born in 1953 pays $271.46.

At the bottom it is capped too, because the credit is non-refundable — a filer at $20,000 gains $23.23 rather than $45.00, since the credit already covered more of their tax than the increase is worth.
Utah cut its rate twice in two years: 4.55% for 2024, 4.5% for 2025 (HB 106), and 4.45% for 2026 (SB 60).

Utah's child tax credit is withdrawn at TEN cents on the dollar — 2.2 times the state's own tax rate, so the withdrawal is a larger marginal tax than the tax is. $1,000 for each child under 6, gone by $59,000 of income for a single filer with one child and $71,000 for a couple ($49,000/$61,000 in 2026 after HB 290, $43,000/$54,000 in 2025). Inside the band a Utah family faces about 14.75% on the next dollar against a headline 4.45%, and 16.05% where the Taxpayer Tax Credit is being withdrawn at the same time.

The child tax credit is withdrawn against a DIFFERENT income figure from Utah's retirement credits, on the same return. TC-40 line 9 — state taxable income, after every Utah subtraction — plus tax-exempt interest, where the Retirement and Social Security Benefits credits use line 6, before them. A Utah subtraction therefore buys back child credit and does nothing for a retiree's.

The credit is per child under 6 and ends the year the child turns 6, so a Utah family loses $1,000 on a birthday and nothing on the return says why. HB 106 (2025) widened it from the 1-to-3 band it had in 2024, where a newborn did not qualify at all.
Not modelled: the Utah credits for at-home parents and 529 contributions. A family claiming either will compute too high here.

Utah's earned income credit is 20% of the federal credit and is NON-REFUNDABLE — Utah Code § 59-10-1044 sits in Part 10, the Nonrefundable Tax Credit Act. It is the only state credit in this package that is a share of the federal credit and cannot be paid out, and the difference is the whole point of the credit for the filers it is aimed at: a Utah single parent whose Taxpayer Tax Credit already wipes out their tax receives nothing from it.

Utah taxes Social Security and then hands the tax back. The Social Security Benefits Credit (code AH, § 59-10-1042) is the state's own rate applied to the part of the benefit § 86 made taxable, so below $90,000 of modified AGI ($54,000 single, $45,000 separate) the benefit costs a Utah retiree nothing — and above it the credit is withdrawn at 2.5 cents on the dollar. SB 71 (2025) raised those thresholds 20% from $75,000/$45,000/$37,500 and they are NOT indexed.

A retiree may claim only ONE side of Utah's retirement credits: the Retirement Credit (code 18) on one side, or the Social Security Benefits Credit (code AH) together with the Military Retirement Credit (code AJ) on the other — § 59-10-1019(5). This engine computes both sides and takes the larger, which is always optimal because a non-refundable credit is worth min(itself, tax remaining) and min is monotone. The result names the side that was taken.

Utah's real marginal rate on a retiree reaches 15.26% — 3.4 times the 4.45% statutory rate — and it is three rules compounding, none of which is a bracket. A dollar of pension drags 85 cents of Social Security into federal AGI under § 86; Utah taxes all $1.85 at 4.45%, withdraws 2.5 cents of AH per dollar of it and 1.3 cents of Taxpayer Tax Credit per dollar of it. 1.85 x 8.25%. For a couple with a $70,000 benefit the rate runs 10.64% -> 15.26% -> 8.25% as income rises, peaking at $90,387.50 of federal AGI and FALLING after it, so the highest-taxed next dollar in Utah belongs to a household in the 12% federal bracket.

Tax-exempt interest is added back for both credits (§ 59-10-1019(1)(b), § 59-10-1042(1)(b)), so a municipal bond is taxed at 2.5% in Utah while appearing on no line of Utah income. For a couple with $40,000 of benefits and $60,000 of pension, $10,000 of exempt interest costs exactly $250.00 of Utah tax and $0.00 of federal tax. Pass it as `taxExemptInterest`; leaving it out understates a bondholding retiree.
